## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="a15-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<!-- a15-ideas:start (written from the model by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<dl class="lx-ideas"><dt>Efficiency as a resource</dt><dd>A saved MWh has a cost: the extra cost spread over the life with the capital recovery factor, plus any extra yearly cost, divided by the MWh saved a year.</dd><dt>The curve</dt><dd>Cheapest first, each block counting what it saves after those to its left, 3 of 4 electricity measures for Prairie City's buildings cost less than Kansas's average price (6%, no rebound).</dd><dt>Rebound</dt><dd>Part of a saving comes back as more comfort; it raises the cost per MWh actually saved.</dd><dt>Peaks, not MWh</dt><dd>All the core's gas heat on heat pumps adds 14% to its year's electricity but 53% to its peak on a design day whose minimum is −18 °C.</dd><dt>Industry by temperature</dt><dd>Heat below about 165 °C suits heat pumps, some low-pressure steam included; hotter steam, ovens and hydrogen need boilers, resistance heating or electrolysis.</dd></dl>
<!-- a15-ideas:end -->
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>The cost of saved energy, by hand</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

A measure costs $C$ more up front and $A$ more a year (upkeep, a fan's electricity), lasts $n$ years and saves $\Delta E$ MWh a year; at a [real discount rate]{.lx-term term="real-rate"} $r$,

$$\text{CSE} = \frac{C \times \text{CRF}(r, n) + A}{\Delta E}, \qquad \text{CRF}(r, n) = \frac{r(1+r)^n}{(1+r)^n - 1}$$

- **[Capital recovery factor]{.lx-term term="capital-recovery-factor"}** turns a cost paid now into equal yearly payments over the life ([A1](a01-project-tea.html)).
- **At replacement or any time.** When old equipment is replaced anyway, count only the extra cost of the efficient choice; a retrofit pays the whole cost.
- **Yardstick.** Here, Kansas's 2025 average retail price, flat per MWh; a customer's own tariff can differ, and a utility compares the CSE with the supply cost it avoids, which this lesson leaves out.
- **Real programs.** U.S. utility programs saved electricity at a total cost of about $0.049 per kWh in 2009–2015 (2016 dollars, LBNL).

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Why the order of measures matters</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **Savings interact.** After a heat pump with seasonal COP $\bar c$, a better [envelope]{.lx-term term="building-envelope"} saves $1/\bar c$ as much electricity, so its CSE rises by $\bar c$ (practice item 4).
- **Packages.** Measures that compete for the same equipment (a condensing furnace or a heat pump) cannot both be counted in full.
- **The curve is a sequence.** Each block counts only what it saves after the blocks to its left, so the widths add up; a different order gives different blocks.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Peaks, design days and substations</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **[Design day]{.lx-term term="design-day"}.** Planners size heating and wires for a cold day that comes back every few years, not the average one.
- **Coincidence.** A district's [coincident peak]{.lx-term term="coincident-peak"} is the most it draws in one hour; when many homes heat at once, it nears the sum of their own peaks.
- **Simplifications.** One substation per district; base load follows SPP's 2025 shape, which already carries some of the region's electric heating, so winter base load runs a little high.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>From closed forms to an optimization</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **Here,** every measure and every switch is set by hand and priced on its own.
- **In a model,** a linear program chooses envelopes, heat pumps, networks and stores together, with each substation's limit as a rule and the hour-by-hour balance of heat and power.
- **Next.** The City Planner sandbox ([SB3](sb3-city-planner.html)) and the city energy hub ([M12](m12-city-model.html)) build that model.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this lesson leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>The grid costs that savings and new peaks avoid or add: generation, wires and capacity.</li>
<li>Substation and feeder upgrade costs, and their timing.</li>
<li>Comfort and health, and the value of the rebound itself.</li>
<li>Cooling: the summer peak, which electrifying heat does not raise.</li>
<li>How fast homes and firms actually adopt each measure.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

<p class="lx-lede">Practice, about 30 minutes: four myths, one question, then seven worked exercises.</p>

<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="a15-myth"><div class="lx-qq" data-id="kwh" data-answer="myth"><p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Electrifying heat only adds kilowatt-hours over the year.”</p><ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. The core's gas heat on heat pumps adds 14% to its year's electricity but 53% to its design-day peak: 212.8 to 325.4 MW.</p></details></div><div class="lx-qq" data-id="cold" data-answer="myth"><p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Heat pumps stop working in a cold snap.”</p><ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. ENERGY STAR's cold-climate criteria ask for a COP of at least 1.75 at −15 °C (5 °F), and this lesson's curve gives 2.29 at −18 °C: efficiency falls, so peaks grow.</p></details></div><div class="lx-qq" data-id="timer" data-answer="myth"><p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Charging cars after midnight always eases the grid.”</p><ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. On the design day a midnight timer puts the suburbs' charging on the coldest hours: 233.0 MW against 199.3 MW as today, with 30% electric cars.</p></details></div><div class="lx-qq" data-id="pays" data-answer="myth"><p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Every efficiency measure pays for itself.”</p><ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Weatherizing an older home with a standard gas furnace saves gas at $105.3 per MWh at 6%, above Kansas's 2025 average gas price, $48.8; comfort and a lower peak are not in that number.</p></details></div></div><div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="a15"><div class="lx-qq" data-id="rebound" data-answer="b"><p class="lx-qtext">A measure saves energy at $40 per MWh with no rebound. With a 25% rebound, what does a saved MWh cost?</p><ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">$30.00</li><li data-value="b">$53.33</li><li data-value="c">$50.00</li></ul><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>$40 ÷ (1 − 0.25) = $53.33: the cost is the same, the MWh saved are a quarter fewer.</p></details></div></div>
<!-- a15-check:end -->
<div class="lx-card a15-practice">
<!-- a15-practice:start (written from the model by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Practice · about 30 minutes on your own</p><ol class="lx-fb-practice"><li><p><b>One measure by hand.</b> What does a saved MWh of gas cost, and does it beat the price?</p><table class="lx-mini-table a15-given"><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Extra purchase cost (a condensing furnace against a standard one)</th><td>$688.01</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Extra a year: upkeep and fan electricity</th><td>$59.87</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Life</th><td>22.5 years</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Gas saved a year</th><td>2.918 MWh</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Real discount rate</th><td>6%</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Gas price (Kansas average, 2025)</th><td>$48.77 per MWh</td></tr></tbody></table><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>CRF = 0.0821; $688.01 × 0.0821 = $56.49, plus $59.87 = $116.36 a year; ÷ 2.918 MWh = $39.88 per MWh, under gas at $48.77.</p></details></li><li><p><b>The discount rate decides.</b> Does it beat the price at a 3% and at a 10% real discount rate?</p><table class="lx-mini-table a15-given"><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Weatherizing an older home heated by resistance (a retrofit)</th><td>$6,875.72</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Life</th><td>20 years</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Electricity saved a year</th><td>4.401 MWh</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Electricity price (Kansas homes' average, 2025)</th><td>$144.40 per MWh</td></tr></tbody></table><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>At 3%: CRF 0.0672, $462.05 a year, $104.99 per MWh, so yes; at 10%: CRF 0.1175, $807.90, $183.57, so no. Near the price, the rate decides.</p></details></li><li><p><b>Rebound.</b> What does a saved MWh cost with the rebound?</p><table class="lx-mini-table a15-given"><tbody><tr><th scope="row">A heat pump replacing resistance heat, no rebound</th><td>$105.67 per MWh saved</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Rebound</th><td>20%</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Electricity price</th><td>$144.40 per MWh</td></tr></tbody></table><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>$105.67 ÷ (1 − 0.20) = $132.09 per MWh, still under $144.40. Rebound shrinks the saving, not the cost.</p></details></li><li><p><b>Interactions.</b> With the heat pump in first, what does weatherization's saved MWh cost?</p><table class="lx-mini-table a15-given"><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Weatherizing a resistance-heated home, on its own</th><td>$136.23 per MWh saved</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Seasonal COP of a heat pump installed first</th><td>3.43</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Electricity price</th><td>$144.40 per MWh</td></tr></tbody></table><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>The heat pump already divides the heat's electricity by 3.43, so weatherization saves that much less: $136.23 × 3.43 = $467.27 per MWh, now over $144.40. The curve's block 4 gives $467.09 with the COP unrounded.</p></details></li><li><p><b>A cold hour.</b> Half the gas and propane heat moves to heat pumps: what is the hour's total load?</p><table class="lx-mini-table a15-given"><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Hour on the design day</th><td>07:00, −15.8 °C</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Heat-pump COP at that hour</th><td>2.37</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">The core's heat need</th><td>371.4 MW</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Base load</th><td>124.4 MW</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Cars charging</th><td>0.2 MW</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Shares of the heat: gas, propane, resistance, heat pumps</th><td>0.693, 0.000, 0.187, 0.120</td></tr></tbody></table><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Heat-pump share 0.120 + (0.693 + 0.000) ÷ 2 = 0.467; 371.4 × (0.187 + 0.467 ÷ 2.37) = 142.6 MW of heating; plus 124.4 MW base and 0.2 MW of cars: 267.2 MW, against 250.</p></details></li><li><p><b>Evening chargers.</b> How much do the suburbs' cars add at 19:00?</p><table class="lx-mini-table a15-given"><tbody><tr><th scope="row">The suburbs' charging a day, 30% electric cars, as today</th><td>271.8 MWh</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Share of a day's charging at 19:00</th><td>10%</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Charging at 19:00 in 2025</th><td>1.01 MW</td></tr></tbody></table><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>271.8 × 0.10 = 27.2 MW, against 1.01 MW in 2025.</p></details></li><li><p><b>Industrial heat pump.</b> How much electricity would heat pumps need, as a steady MW?</p><table class="lx-mini-table a15-given"><tbody><tr><th scope="row">The park's heat below 100 °C</th><td>140,000 MWh a year</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Heat-pump COP</th><td>2.5</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Hours in a year</th><td>8,760</td></tr></tbody></table><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>140,000 ÷ 2.5 = 56,000 MWh a year; ÷ 8,760 h = 6.4 MW.</p></details></li></ol>
<!-- a15-practice:end -->
</div>
